about: The Individual Research Project (MATH40008) is a 5-ECTS core module in Term 3 of Imperial's Mathematics BSc, taken after the end-of-year exams. Each student explores an area of mathematics, chosen from options offered by project supervisors, and produces and presents a poster on it: the assessed presentation is typically about 5 minutes, followed by a longer discussion session. It is pass/fail only and does not count towards the year total, and the poster and oral components must each be passed separately (2026–27 handbook). There is no fixed syllabus, so this pack explains the format and how to prepare; the advice on research, poster design and presenting is general good practice, not official requirements.

notes.h: What the project is and how it is assessed
notes.body:
The Individual Research Project (MATH40008) closes the first year of Imperial's Mathematics BSc. It is not a taught course with a syllabus and exam. Instead, you spend the end of the year investigating one area of mathematics on your own and presenting what you found.

Confirmed facts (2026–27 handbook and the department's first-year course page)
- It is a 5-ECTS core module in Term 3, with roughly 6 lectures and 6 classes.
- It follows the end-of-year exams.
- Its aim is to develop elementary research skills in mathematics while you explore a specific area that interests you. The department's course page says the topic is chosen from options offered by project supervisors.
- Each student produces a poster on their chosen area and presents it.
- The assessed presentation of the poster typically lasts about 5 minutes. You are also expected to be available to discuss your poster with other students and staff during a longer session.
- The module is pass/fail only and does not contribute to the year total.
- The poster and the oral component must each be passed separately: a strong poster cannot make up for a failed presentation, or the other way round.
- Formative feedback comes in tutorials and workshops. Summative feedback is given as comments on your poster and presentation.

What this means for you
- Because the module is pass/fail, the aim is a clear, correct and well-explained piece of work rather than chasing marks. But you still have to pass both parts.
- The handbook does not publish detailed marking criteria, word limits or a poster size in its module entry. Treat the module's own briefing materials and the workshops as the authority on these, and follow any template you are given.
- Many mathematicians produce posters in LaTeX (for example with a poster class), and learning it now will help later projects. Use whatever tool your briefing allows.

Exam tips: there is no written exam, so plan your time like a mini-project: choose early, read actively, draft the poster with time for feedback, and rehearse the talk out loud.

The project asks you to do on a small scale what mathematicians do all the time: pick a question, read around it, understand one piece properly and explain it. This note gives general advice; follow your supervisor's guidance where it differs.

Choosing well
- Pick something you are curious about and can understand with first-year tools. A narrow topic explained properly is better than a broad survey you can only describe.
- Good shapes for a first-year topic: one theorem with a clear proof and examples; one method with a worked application; or one surprising example and why it works.
- Check early that there are accessible sources: textbook chapters, expository articles or lecture notes at the right level.

Reading mathematics actively
- Read with pen and paper. Re-derive each step, test definitions on small examples, and draw pictures.
- For each theorem, write down the exact hypotheses and find out what goes wrong if one is dropped. A counterexample is often the clearest way to show you understand a result.
- Keep a log of definitions, results and the sources they came from as you go, so that writing up is easier.

Working with a supervisor
- Arrive at meetings with specific questions ("I don't follow this step", "is this example appropriate?") rather than general ones.
- Show drafts early. Feedback on a rough poster is far more useful than feedback on a finished one.

Academic integrity
- Everything on the poster must be your own explanation. Quote sparingly and cite every source you rely on, including diagrams you adapt.
- If you use software or AI tools, follow the department's and College's current rules on their use and say what you used where required.
- Check that every statement on the poster is correct. A wrong theorem statement or a gap in a proof is the kind of error that examiners notice.

A simple plan
- Days 1–2: choose and narrow the topic; collect two or three sources.
- Next few days: understand the core result, work through examples, and decide on the one main message.
- Then: draft the poster, get feedback, revise, and rehearse the talk.
Adjust this to the actual dates in your briefing.

Exam tips: be able to state your main result precisely and explain why it is true in two minutes, because that is what the discussion session will probe.

A research poster is read standing up, in a few minutes, often while you are talking. Its job is to communicate one idea clearly, not to reproduce a report. The advice below is general good practice; any template, size or format in your briefing takes priority.

Structure
- Title: specific and informative (for example "Why there are infinitely many primes: three proofs" rather than "Prime numbers").
- Motivation: one short paragraph saying what the question is and why it is interesting.
- Core: the key definitions, the main result stated precisely, and the idea of the proof or method.
- Example or application: a worked example, picture or computation that makes the result concrete.
- Conclusion: what the reader should remember, and perhaps an open question or extension.
- References: the sources you used.

Making the mathematics readable
- State definitions and theorems in full, with all hypotheses.
- Give proof sketches that show the key idea; full routine details can be left for the conversation.
- Use diagrams and examples generously. A good picture often replaces a paragraph.
- Use notation consistently and define every symbol the first time it appears.

Layout
- Arrange the content in columns that read top to bottom and left to right.
- Use large text, with headings readable from a distance, and plenty of white space.
- Prefer short paragraphs and lists to dense prose.
- Keep colours and fonts consistent, and make sure figures have captions.

Tools
- LaTeX poster classes (such as tikzposter or beamerposter) give good mathematical typesetting.
- Some people use presentation or design software instead; if you do, check how equations will be typeset.
- Print or view the poster at full size before submitting, to check that text is legible and nothing has moved.

Checking before submission
- Ask a friend from the course to read the poster without you and tell you the main message. If they can't, simplify.
- Proofread every formula. Check that the theorem statements match your sources.

Exam tips: aim for one clear story. If something does not support your main message, cut it; you can mention it in conversation.

notes.h: The oral presentation and poster session
notes.body:
The oral component must be passed separately from the poster, so treat it as seriously as the poster itself. The handbook says the assessed presentation typically takes around 5 minutes, followed by a longer session in which you discuss your poster with students and staff.

Planning a five-minute talk
- Five minutes is short: roughly one minute of motivation, two to three minutes on the main result and idea, and one minute on an example and conclusion.
- Use the poster as your visual aid: point to the parts you are discussing, in order.
- Decide on the one thing your audience should remember, and say it clearly at the start and the end.

Rehearsing
- Practise out loud several times, with a timer, and adjust so that you finish comfortably within the time.
- Present to a friend and ask them what was unclear.
- Do not read a script. Notes with a few key phrases help you stay on track while still talking naturally.

Handling questions
- Expect questions such as "Why is this hypothesis needed?", "Can you give an example?", "Where does the proof use this fact?" and "What would you look at next?".
- It is fine to pause and think, and to say what you do and do not know. A careful "I'm not sure, but I think it fails because…" is better than a confident wrong answer.
- Be ready to work through a small example on paper or on a whiteboard if one is available.

The longer discussion session
- Stand by your poster and be ready to give a short version of your talk to each new visitor.
- Adapt the level to the listener: a fellow student may want the big picture, while a member of staff may ask about details of the proof.

Practicalities
- Check the time, place and any required format in your briefing, and arrive early.
- Bring any notes you are allowed and have a printed copy of your references handy.

Exam tips: the best preparation is to explain your topic to someone else several times before the day, until you can do it clearly without looking at the poster.

questions.q: According to the 2026–27 handbook, what is needed to pass the Individual Research Project (MATH40008)?
options: Passing the poster and the oral component separately
An average of at least 40% across the poster and the oral component
Passing the poster alone, with the presentation for feedback only
An overall mark of at least 50%, with several attempts allowed
questions.why: The handbook says both the poster and the oral component must be passed separately. Averaging the two parts assumes a strong poster can compensate for a weak talk, which the separate-pass rule does not allow. Treating the presentation as feedback-only ignores that the oral component is assessed. The 50% pass mark with several attempts is the rule for Introduction to University Mathematics (MATH40001), not this module.

questions.q: How does MATH40008 contribute to the Year 1 total?
options: It counts in proportion to its 5 ECTS
Only the poster mark counts, because the talk is pass/fail
It does not: it is pass/fail only
It counts like the 10-ECTS core modules
questions.why: The handbook lists the module as pass/fail only, so its mark does not contribute to the year total. Treating it like the 10-ECTS core modules confuses it with weighted modules such as Calculus and Applications. Counting it by its 5 ECTS assumes credits determine the weighting, but this module has weight 0. Saying only the poster mark counts assumes the poster is graded differently from the talk, but the whole module, poster included, is pass/fail.
